name: ALH 84001 (Mars meteorite)
short_description: Not an organism: a 1931 g lump of Martian orthopyroxenite found in the Allan Hills, Antarctica, on 27 December 1984. In 1996 a NASA team led by David McKay reported four findings in it that together looked like traces of past life; every one now has a non-biological explanation. The atlas closes here because the testing is the lesson, not the claim.
_what_is_depicted: This subject is a rock, so none of the four images is a micrograph of an organism and none of them may assert that anything here is alive. The four styles were composed as one scale ladder rather than four views of one body: 3d = the hand specimen as a museum object (what ALH 84001 actually is); textbook = a cutaway block of the rock carrying both the carbonate globule and the fracture-surface texture (where the 1996 claim was located); watercolor = the same globule as a mineralogical plate, in cross-section in its pyroxene setting; sem = the segmented shape at nanometre scale, which is the modality the famous 1996 image actually is. The segmented shape is rendered in every style as welded mineral relief — a fused row of knobs, half sunk, with the surrounding grains banked against its flanks and no shadow beneath it — never as a body lying on a surface.

textbook.1: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). The almond-shaped wedge with a concentric orange disc centred in it read as an EYE — pointed at both ends, iris and pupil. Unusable on a subject whose one hard rule is that nothing may look alive. Specimen also small in frame and drawn with heavy cartoon outlines.
textbook.2: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). Silhouette fixed — a proper rectangular block with a crack across it — but the concretion's band order came back INVERTED: a radial scan outward from its middle gave near-black at the centre and cream-white outside, i.e. the Fe/S band that carries the magnetite put in the core instead of the rim. The segmented welt was drawn resting on the granular patch with a shadow under it, reading as a caterpillar.
textbook.3: FAIL (gemini-3-pro-image). Band order now correct and the welt embedded, but the block's CUT SIDES were drawn as horizontal orange-brown sedimentary strata. ALH 84001 is an igneous cumulate; layered bedding is a plain science error, not a style quibble. The magnesite crystal crown had also become a continuous sunburst ring.
textbook.4: PASS, chosen (gemini-3-pro-image). Measured, not judged. Radial pixel scan outward from the concretion centre at (410,515) going up: RGB(160,82,44) burnt-orange for r=0-21, (206,140,96)→(228,184,135) apricot for r=24-48, (69,67,62) near-black at r=57-63, (245,235,219) cream-white at r=66-69, (65,61,54) near-black at r=78, then (141,150,132) greenish-grey rock from r=84 — all five bands, in the correct outward order, with the magnetite-bearing dark band in the rim where it belongs. The same coarse interlocking crystal mosaic runs over the top face AND down both cut sides in the same colours, with no bedding or stripes anywhere. Edge bands: all four are uniform charcoal, mean RGB 57-58, std <1.1, min 54 — no border, frame or vignette. 3x3 magnified contact sheet at 2x: no lettering, digits, scale bar or watermark in any tile. In the upper-right granular patch the segmented welt is a short row of fused knobs, half sunk, with grit banked against both flanks and no shadow line under it. COMPROMISE RECORDED: the concretion is drawn standing slightly proud of the fracture face with a faint drop shadow, rather than cut flush. Attempt 5 tried to fix that and produced a worse result (see below), so this was accepted and re-read against the literature instead: carbonate in ALH 84001 also occurs as 'minute thin pancakes found attached to broken surfaces' (McKay et al. 1996; Scott et al. 1998), so a zoned pancake sitting on the fracture face is a documented habit and the label says so.
textbook.5: FAIL (gemini-3-pro-image). The 'cut flush' clause improved the painterly shading within each grain but gave the concretion a ring of small facets that read as LEGS — the disc came back looking like a small turtle or beetle sitting on the rock. On this subject that is disqualifying, so attempt 4 was kept.

sem.1: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). The surface came back as a flat slate plane with rounded tan spheres strewn on it in loose clusters. Isolated same-size tan spheres on grey read as cocci microcolonies, which is the exact misreading this subject cannot afford.
sem.2: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). 'Packed shoulder to shoulder' did not move it — still a flat plate with scattered spheres, and the ridge had become a meandering chain of separate beads following a crack, reading more like a biofilm than less. Diagnosis: colouring the knobs tan against a grey ground was what made them read as separate bodies.
sem.3: PASS, chosen (gemini-3-pro-image). The fix was to tie the false colour to HEIGHT rather than to objects ('everything low is slate blue-grey, every high point is warm ochre, continuous gradient between'), so no colour boundary marks out a body. The whole frame is one continuous rubble crust: blunt broken knobs and angular crystal facets of many sizes jammed together, mounds and terraces, deep shadowed clefts, splintered plates jutting out. At 2x magnification the central ridge shows flat crystal facets and sharp fractured edges, carries the same dusty crystalline speckle as the crust around it, and its lower flank merges continuously into the neighbouring knobs — no undercut, no shadow gap, no membrane, no plumpness. Modality-correct: SEM shows surface only and there is no interior anywhere in the frame. Edge bands are all image content (means 68-131, std 35-64); no dark continuous line, no letterbox. Two magnified crops (centre and lower right) checked: no lettering, no scale bar, no NASA-style caption.

3d.1: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). Specimen too small in frame and roughly square in outline rather than markedly wider than tall; the exposed interior read as flat mosaic tiles pasted on, not crystal relief.
3d.2: PARTIAL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). Size, aspect and framing all correct and it reads unmistakably as a rock, but the break face was still flat tiling and the crust was smooth rather than hackly. Kept as fallback.
3d.3: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). Crystal relief arrived but the exterior smoothed into a rounded river cobble, losing the weathered meteorite crust, and the grains became free-standing euhedral crystals in a cavity — a geode druse, not a cumulate. ALH 84001's interior is a tightly interlocking granular mass.
3d.4: PASS, chosen (gemini-3-pro-image). Checked against the real NASA specimen photographs (S85-39565 and the second JSC frame, both PD) and against the ANSMET field description quoted in the Martian Meteorite Compendium: 'highly-shocked, grayish-green achondrite, 90% covered with fusion crust', the crust 'spalled in some areas from the hackly end, exposing a uniform coarse-grained rock with a greenish-gray color and a blocky texture'. The render matches that: a loaf-shaped lump about half again as wide as it is tall, spanning ~4/5 of the frame width; matte dark grey-brown crust with pale beige dust, torn scallops and stepped flakes over roughly two thirds of the surface; the right-hand third flaked away in a ragged step exposing tightly interlocking greenish-grey blocky crystals at many angles with hard cleavage glints, black chromite specks and small rust-orange flecks along the grain boundaries. Natural stone tones, no neon, no gloss. Edge bands: pale studio grey, means 202-226, std 2.3-11.9, min 176 — no dark border anywhere. 3x3 magnified sheet: no lettering, no scale cube, no caption. Nothing cell-like, nothing glowing, no space imagery.

watercolor.1: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). The worst render of the batch and the reason the whole approach was rethought: an oval slab with a ring of same-size polygons around a concentric orange middle reads as a CELL with a wall and a nucleus. On the atlas's one non-living subject that is disqualifying.
watercolor.2: FAIL (gemini-2.5-flash-image). Angular slab and a through-going crack fixed the cell reading, but the slab floated as an island with a dark wash halo all round it, and a radial scan again gave the band order INVERTED (near-black in the middle, cream-white outside).
watercolor.3: FAIL (gemini-3-pro-image). Band order finally correct, but the magnesite crystal crown was drawn as a continuous fine sunburst ring right round the circumference, which turns the concretion into a diatom or a sun; and the slab still ended on the paper on all four sides instead of running off two edges.
watercolor.4: FAIL (gemini-3-pro-image). Edges and crown both fixed, but the concretion was placed straddling the slab's broken margin, so half of it hung over bare paper — a concretion has to be enclosed in stone.
watercolor.5: PASS, chosen (gemini-3-pro-image). Radial pixel scan outward from the concretion centre at (635,528) going up: RGB(137,84,38)→(210,112,37) burnt-orange for r=0-36, (240,171,102)→(228,198,151) apricot for r=39-63, (91,84,65)/(119,111,92) dark band at r=66-75, (247,230,201) cream-white at r=78-87, (55,42,21)/(61,40,19) near-black at r=90-99, then pale grain wash from r=102 — five bands, correct outward order. The concretion sits well inside the body of the slab with stone all round it, roughly one sixth of the visible slab width, and the crack demonstrably enters it on the upper left and leaves on the lower right, so it reads as a fracture filling rather than a nucleus. Crystal facets appear only in two or three short irregular stretches, not as a ring — no starburst. The slab runs off the LEFT and BOTTOM edges (left edge band mean RGB 184/164/120, bottom 193/176/136 — stone, not paper) while the top and right edges are paper (234/210/168), so the plate is cropped rather than matted; no sheet-on-a-surface, no mat, no frame. The sepia stain enters at the upper right as an uneven blotch and never closes into a ring. 3x3 magnified sheet: no lettering anywhere; the outer dark band is visibly speckled with darker grains, which is the magnetite and sulfide it is supposed to carry.

reference: PASS, and it is the honest reference for this subject because the 1996 claim IS this picture. Downloaded and viewed: NASA/JSC frame 96-12609, the 'Mars worm' scanning electron micrograph of a fracture surface in ALH 84001, greyscale, public domain as a work of NASA, via Wikimedia Commons (File:ALH84001_structures.jpg, 1983x1351). APOD credits it to D. McKay (NASA/JSC), K. Thomas-Keprta (Lockheed-Martin), R. Zare (Stanford), NASA. MODALITY: SEM — a scanning electron micrograph of rock, not a photograph of a specimen and not a light micrograph of an organism. WHAT IT SHOWS: a knobbly granular mineral surface with one elongated segmented ridge running diagonally across it and several bright angular mineral fragments. That ridge is the DISPUTED shape — it is not a confirmed fossil, and this atlas does not present it as one. PROVENANCE CAVEAT worth stating plainly: this specific frame was released by NASA on 9 August 1996 and was NOT one of the figures in the 16 August 1996 Science paper. NASA's own caption says so: 'Although this structure is not part of the research published in the Aug. 16 issue of the journal Science, it is located in a similar carbonate glob in the meteorite.' It is the image that carried the story to the public, not a figure from the paper. PROCESSING: deterministic centre crop of the 1351-pixel-tall square region plus LANCZOS resize to 1080 — a DOWNSCALE of 0.80x, no upscaling. edit_image.py was deliberately not run: the source carries no text, no scale bar, no border and no letterbox, so there was nothing to strip and any edit risked re-illustrating a historically important frame. The crop keeps the segmented ridge running through the centre of the square. Other freely-licensed images were found and are recorded in research.json rather than shipped: the PD NASA hand-specimen photographs S85-39565 and File:ALH84001.jpg (both carry baked-in 'ALH84001,0' lettering and a '1cm.' scale cube), a PD USGS close-up of the fracture surface, and two CC BY-SA Smithsonian display photographs. The hand-specimen frames were used as depiction guides for the 3d style.
decision: The anchor image of the set and the one that states the subject: this is a rock. Matched against the real NASA specimen photographs and the ANSMET field description — grey-brown hackly fusion crust over most of the surface, spalled at one end to expose a coarse greenish-grey blocky interior. Labelled, because the crust / spalled break / interior distinction is exactly what a reader needs.

The primary labelled figure. Carries the whole argument in one frame: the igneous matrix, the fracture, the zoned carbonate globule with its magnetite-bearing dark rim, and the segmented shape as a texture of the stone. Band order verified by radial pixel scan on the raw PNG. Compromise: the globule stands slightly proud of the fracture face rather than cut flush — accepted as the documented 'pancake attached to a broken surface' habit rather than corrected, after attempt 5 made it worse.

The globule at mineral scale, as a 19th-century mineralogical plate. Chosen over a painted hand specimen so that the four styles form a scale ladder instead of two duplicate rock portraits. Labelled with black ink on a paper halo. The crack passing through the globule is doing real work here: it is what stops a concentric orange oval from reading as a cell.

The modality of the claim itself, and deliberately the plainest image in the set: nothing but stone. Not labelled — pointing at the ridge with a leader line and a caption is the job of the textbook figure, where the word CLAIMED can sit next to the matrix and the globule that give it context. On its own the SEM is presented as what it is, a rugged mineral surface with one welded ridge on it.
compromises: textbook: the carbonate globule stands slightly proud of the fracture face with a faint drop shadow instead of being cut flush. Defensible as the 'thin pancake attached to a broken surface' habit (McKay 1996, Scott 1998) and labelled accordingly, but it is not what the prompt asked for.

All four styles show the segmented shape or its setting at a size a reader cannot calibrate: nothing in the pictures conveys that the real shapes are 20-100 nm. That number lives in the labels and the text only.

The textbook and watercolour globules are drawn with five clean concentric bands. Real rosettes are oscillatory and messy, and the compendium's own compiler notes that 'the exact nature of the black rims has not been properly characterized'. The renders show the idealised textbook version.
The magnesite rim's outward-projecting crystal faces are drawn on only part of the circumference to avoid a starburst; in the rock they occur all round.
No render shows PAHs or the 2022 serpentinisation result — those are chemistry, not morphology, and are carried entirely by the text.
renders_burned: 17 style renders (textbook 5, watercolor 5, 3d 4, sem 3) + 2 coloring renders = 19 image API calls. The coloring page's final artwork came from a local crop-and-re-trace of coloring attempt 2, which cost no call. Estimated spend: $0.735 on the style renders (from the sidecars) plus ~$0.08 on the coloring renders.
models: gemini-2.5-flash-image for attempts 1-2 on every style (and attempt 3 on 3d); gemini-3-pro-image for every accepted render. No Imagen tier was used. No 429 / quota failure occurred.
